procedural_history.originating_court: Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Khurja, Bulandshahar
procedural_history.impugned_order: Summoning order dated 28.02.2023 passed by the Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Khurja, Bulandshahar in Complaint Case No. 547 of 2021, for offences punishable under Sections 406 and 420 of the Indian Penal Code.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants filed Application No. 15453 of 2023 in the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad seeking to quash and set aside the summoning order. The High Court rejected the application on 03.04.2024.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court after the High Court declined to quash the summoning order. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal.

directions: The impugned order passed by the High Court is set aside so also the order passed by the Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Khurja, Bulandshahar taking cognizance upon the complaint.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in declining to quash the summoning order passed by the Magistrate against the company and its office bearers for offences punishable under Sections 406 and 420 of the IPC.

facts: A private complaint was filed against a company and its office bearers for offences under Sections 406 (criminal breach of trust) and 420 (cheating) of the IPC, alleging non-payment for goods.
The Magistrate issued a summoning order against the company and its office bearers for the offence under Section 406 IPC.
The accused (the company and its bearers) filed an application in the High Court under Section 482 of the CrPC to quash the summoning order.
The High Court rejected this application, upholding the Magistrate's order.
law: The Indian Penal Code (IPC) does not contain any provision for attaching vicarious liability to the office bearers of a company for offences like criminal breach of trust (S. 406) or cheating (S. 420).
For office bearers to be held criminally liable, the complaint must contain direct and specific allegations demonstrating their personal involvement in the offence.
Vicarious liability for company officers can only be imposed if a specific statute explicitly provides for it.
A Magistrate must apply their mind to the complaint to determine if a prima facie criminal offence is disclosed before taking cognizance and issuing a summoning order.

The High Court has the power under Section 482 CrPC to quash proceedings if the complaint does not disclose the commission of an offence or if the summoning order was passed without application of mind.
application: The Supreme Court found a "total non-application of mind" by both the Magistrate and the High Court.

The Magistrate failed to consider the crucial question of whether the office bearers could be held personally liable, especially since the IPC does not provide for vicarious liability for these offences.
The complaint lacked the necessary direct allegations against the office bearers to show their personal culpability in any cheating or criminal breach of trust.
The Supreme Court noted that the Magistrate should have scrutinized the complaint more carefully before issuing the process.
The High Court completely overlooked this fundamental legal issue regarding vicarious liability when it rejected the petition to quash the summons.
Furthermore, the Court observed that the complaint did not even make out the basic ingredients for the offence of cheating, suggesting the dispute was civil in nature.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in declining to quash the summoning order. The order was legally unsustainable because it wrongly imputed vicarious liability to the company's office bearers, a concept not supported by the Indian Penal Code for these offences, and was issued without a proper application of mind to the facts and law.

issue.issue_text: Whether a Magistrate, at the stage of taking cognizance and issuing process, is obligated to apply his mind to the complaint to determine if sufficient grounds exist for proceeding against the accused.

law.fact: The act of 'taking cognizance' of an offense under Section 190 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not a mechanical act but requires the application of the Magistrate's mind.
law.source: “…before it can be said that any magistrate has taken cognizance of any offence under s. 190(1)(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, he must not only have applied his mind to the contents of the petition, but he must have done so for the purpose of proceeding in a particular way…”

law.fact: A Magistrate is not a 'post office' and cannot issue process as a matter of course. The order must show satisfaction that the allegations constitute an offense and that there are sufficient grounds for proceeding.
law.source: “In other words, the Magistrate is not to act as a post office in taking cognizance of each and every complaint filed before him and issue process as a matter of course. There must be sufficient indication in the order passed by the Magistrate that he is satisfied that the allegations in the complaint constitute an offence…”

law.fact: Summoning an accused in a criminal case is a serious matter that affects a person's dignity and reputation; therefore, the process should not be used as a tool for harassment.
law.source: “To be called to appear before criminal court as an accused is serious matter affecting one’s dignity, self respect and image in society. Hence, the process of criminal court shall not be made a weapon of harassment.”

law.fact: The Magistrate's duty includes carefully scrutinizing the evidence, and they may even question the complainant and witnesses to ascertain the truthfulness of the allegations and determine if a prima facie case is made out.
law.source: “The Magistrate has to carefully scrutinise the evidence brought on record and may even himself put questions to the complainant and his witnesses to elicit answers to find out the truthfulness of the allegations or otherwise and then examine if any offence is prima facie committed…”

law.fact: The Magistrate's inquiry is limited to determining if a prima facie case exists for the purpose of issuing process, not to conduct a detailed examination of the merits to decide if a conviction is likely.
law.source: “It is by now well settled that at the stage of issuing process it is not the duty of the Court to find out as to whether the accused will be ultimately convicted or acquitted. The object of consideration of the merits of the case at this stage could only be to determine whether there are sufficient grounds for proceeding further or not.”

application.fact: The Court applied the principle that taking cognizance is a judicial act, not a clerical one. It reasoned that because summoning an accused is a serious step with significant consequences, a Magistrate cannot simply accept a complaint at face value.
application.source: “Summoning of an accused in a criminal case is a serious matter. Criminal law cannot be set into motion as a matter of course.”

application.fact: The Court emphasized that the Magistrate must act as a gatekeeper to the criminal justice system. This requires a thorough examination of the complaint and evidence to filter out cases that lack sufficient grounds, are of a civil nature, or are patently absurd.
application.source: “If, however, a bare perusal of a complaint or the evidence led in support of it shows essential ingredients of the offences alleged are absent or that the dispute is only of a civil nature or that there are such patent absurdities in evidence produced that it would be a waste of time to proceed further, then of course, the complaint is liable to be dismissed at that stage only.”

application.fact: The Court held that this duty to apply one's mind is so fundamental that it exists even at the pre-cognizance stage (e.g., when ordering a police investigation) and becomes even more critical when the Magistrate is actually taking cognizance and deciding to issue process against an accused.
application.source: “If at the stage of pre-cognizance, the Magistrate is expected to be careful or to put it in other words, the Magistrate is obliged to look into the complaint threadbare so as to reach to a prima facie conclusion, then he is expected to be more careful when he is actually taking cognizance upon a private complaint and ordering issue of process.”

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a Magistrate is absolutely obligated to apply his mind to the complaint and supporting evidence before taking cognizance and issuing process. This is a crucial judicial function to determine if there are sufficient grounds and a prima facie case to proceed against the accused, thereby preventing the misuse of the criminal justice system for harassment.

issue.issue_text: Whether office bearers of a company can be held vicariously liable for offences under the Indian Penal Code in the absence of a specific statutory provision to that effect.

law.fact_text: The Indian Penal Code (IPC) does not contain any specific provision that attaches vicarious liability to the office bearers of a company for offences committed by the company.
For vicarious liability of office bearers to arise in a criminal case, a specific provision must exist in the relevant statute.

Office bearers can only be held liable for offences like cheating or criminal breach of trust under the IPC if there are direct and specific allegations against them, demonstrating their personal involvement and criminal intent (mens rea).

application.fact_text: The Court found that the lower courts failed to consider whether the office bearers were personally liable for any offence, as distinct from the company's liability.

Since the Indian Penal Code lacks a provision for vicarious liability, the Court determined there was no basis to attribute the company's alleged offence of cheating or criminal breach of trust to its office bearers simply because of their positions.
The complainant had not made the necessary direct allegations to show that the office bearers had personally practiced any deception or cheating.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the principle of holding company office bearers vicariously liable for offences under the Indian Penal Code. It held that such liability can only be imposed if a statute explicitly provides for it. In the absence of such a provision in the IPC, an office bearer can only be prosecuted if there are direct allegations and evidence of their personal involvement in the crime.

appellant_arguments: The dispute is civil in nature, and the complainant should have filed a civil suit for recovery of the amount instead of a criminal complaint for cheating and criminal breach of trust.
respondent_arguments: The summoning order was correctly passed based on the facts, circumstances, and evidence on record, such as uncontroverted invoices.

cases.case_name: Mehmood Ul Rehman v. Khazir Mohammad Tunda
cases.principle: Issuance of summons is a serious matter and should not be done mechanically; it should only be done upon satisfaction that there is a ground for proceeding further against a person based on materials collected during the inquiry.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An order issuing a summons is liable to be set aside if it does not provide reasons for the conclusion that there is a prima facie case against the accused, as the formation of an opinion on the existence of a 'sufficient ground for proceeding' requires due application of mind which must be reflected in the order itself.
obiter: A complaint may be quashed where it suffers from fundamental legal defects, such as want of sanction or absence of a complaint by a legally competent authority.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court's core finding is that even if the entire case of the complainant is accepted as true, no criminal offence is disclosed. The dispute is fundamentally civil in nature, arising from the non-payment for goods supplied. The complaint does not disclose the commission of a cognizable offense, and therefore, the Magistrate's order issuing summons is unsustainable in law.
legal_tests_applied: When issuing a summons under Section 204 Cr.P.C., a Magistrate must form an opinion after due application of mind that there is a 'sufficient ground for proceeding' against the accused, and this should not be done mechanically.
An order issuing process is liable to be set aside if no reason is given for the conclusion that there is a prima facie case against the accused, or if the reason given is ex facie incorrect.
A Magistrate's order cannot be sustained in law if the underlying complaint does not disclose the commission of a cognizable offense.
policy_considerations: The continuation of a criminal proceeding in circumstances where the dispute is clearly civil in nature and the complaint discloses no real offense would be nothing but an abuse of the process of law.
